newsitem.title: UK: Green LPG fuel to be introduced to U.K. forecourts.
newsitem.headline: Green LPG fuel to be introduced to U.K. forecourts.

text.p: British motorists will soon be able to top up their tanks with environmentally friendly liquified petroleum gas (LPG) at service stations across the country, Calor Group Plc and petrol retailer Jet said on Thursday.

"Jet outlets in Leeds, Bradford, Birmingham, Staines and London have been selected as the first in a network of service stations to sell the green road fuel, LPG," the companies said in a joint statement.
"The LPG will be dispensed from a forecourt pump alongside petrol, diesel and unleaded fuels," they said.
Recent studies have shown LPG -- which is more familiar to most British consumers as the fuel used in camping lamps and cookers -- produces far lower engine emissions than other motor fuels.
"Tried and tested as a clean fuel, research has proven that LPG reduces particulate emissions by over 95 percent," Calor and Jet, the retail arm of U.S.-based Conoco, said.

They expected initial take-up of the fuel to be highest among local operators of light commercial vehicles, such as taxis and small vans. A number of fleet operators have already started using LPG, they said.
"In the U.K., Calor and Jet are working with a number of public and private fleet operators who have successfully switched to LPG, together with the ambulance and police services," they said.
Critics of LPG as a motor fuel say it will be slow to catch on due to the costs of converting vehicles to its use, but Calor and Jet said this would be cushioned by the lower costs of the fuel.

"Costs to convert a petrol engine to run in parallel with existing fuel start from 1,100 stg," they said. "The vehicle's boot-mounted LPG tank gives a similar mileage range to petrol without taking up significant space."
"In addition to lower fuel prices, drivers will also benefit from improved engine performance as a clean burning fuel contributes to less wear and tear," they said.
Calor and Jet said their promotion of LPG tied in with the moves by the British government to cut harmful motor emissions.
"In the November budget the chancellor made a 25 percent reduction in duty on road fuel gases. Meanwhile duty on petrol and diesel continues to rise," they noted.
